pinterest.title: Japanese Wedding Traditions: Yuinō, San-san-kudo, the Shiromuku and the Bride's Letter
pinterest.description: Japanese wedding traditions follow two families from start to finish. Yuinō, the betrothal gift exchange, opens the story. The Shinto ceremony brings vows spoken to the kami and san-san-kudo, sake shared from three cups. The bride wears a white shiromuku, then changes into colour for the hirōen reception, with goshūgi, kagami biraki and the bride's letter to her parents. Our guide walks through each custom in wedding order, for Australian couples marrying in Japan or at home.

pinterest.title: San-san-kudo: The Three-Cup Sake Ritual at a Japanese Shinto Wedding
pinterest.description: San-san-kudo is the moment most guests remember at a Japanese wedding. The bride and groom drink sake in turn from three flat cups, small, medium and large, served by a miko, the shrine maiden. At many weddings the parents drink too, and the cups pass between the two families. Couples marrying in Australia often keep san-san-kudo even without a shrine: ask your celebrant where it fits in the ceremony, and buy a proper set of cups well ahead.

pinterest.title: Shiromuku to Iro-uchikake: The Japanese Bride's Change of Colour
pinterest.description: A Japanese bride wears white from head to toe for the ceremony: a heavy white outer kimono, the shiromuku, with a wataboshi hood or tsunokakushi band. Before the reception she changes into a brightly coloured iro-uchikake, often red, and some brides later change again into a Western gown. This is oiro-naoshi, the change of colour. Flying cranes, a favourite motif, are symbols of longevity. Build every outfit change into the run sheet, with a dresser on hand.

slides: Japanese wedding traditions you did not know, in wedding order
Yuinō comes first: the two families exchange gifts to mark the engagement, each wrapped and tied with mizuhiki cords.
At the Shinto ceremony, the couple speak their vows to the kami. Close family sit on either side of the hall.
San-san-kudo: the bride and groom drink sake in turn from three flat cups, served by a miko.
The bride wears a white shiromuku for the ceremony, then changes into a brightly coloured iro-uchikake for the reception.
At the hirōen, guests give goshūgi in a formal envelope and leave with hikidemono, the couple's gifts in return.
The couple open a sake barrel together for kagami biraki. Near the end, the bride reads a letter to her parents.

instagram_carousel.caption:
A Japanese wedding is a meeting of two families as much as two people, and parents are present at every stage.

The families exchange yuinō gifts tied with mizuhiki. The couple speak their vows to the kami and share sake from three cups in san-san-kudo. The bride moves from a white shiromuku to a brightly coloured iro-uchikake, and at many weddings to a Western gown as well. At the reception, guests hand in goshūgi at the desk, the couple break open a sake barrel with wooden mallets, and the bride reads a letter to her parents that brings the room to tears.

Customs vary from family to family and region to region, so the best first step is a simple one: ask both families early which moments matter most to them.

Our guide walks through each custom in wedding order: yuinō, the Shinto ceremony and san-san-kudo, the shiromuku and the change of kimono, the chapel ceremony many couples add, then the hirōen with its gifts, its sake barrel, its speeches and senbazuru, a thousand paper cranes. It closes with what Australian couples need to know about marrying in Japan, or bringing these customs home.
